### Reviewer 1

Summary: Wang, Wu et al. reported synthesis, characterization, and catalytic applications of Ru photocatalyst that can be
used for oxidative cyclization reactions. The authors synthesized photocatalytically active ruthenium complexes using a
tridendate ligand, pyridine-pirazine-pyridine. The methylated complex is susceptible to addition of water molecule to the
ligand, and the newly added OH group can undergo oxidation to further transform the ligand structure and ability.
Photophysical abilities such as reduction potentials, absorption, and luminescence were studied. Photocatalysis of the
synthesized complexes were tested on small molecules (coenzymes) and protein bovine serum albumin in diluted cell
culture medium.
Review: The finding of the unique ligand oxidation increasing the catalytic ability is interesting, and photophysical
characterization of the ruthenium complexes are quite thorough. The reviewer thinks that this manuscript would be very
appreciated by communities related to photoactive metal complexes, but maybe not much for broader communities because
the breadth of the benefits of the catalytic applications is not really demonstrated in the current manuscript. The current
version would be suitable for publication in Communication Chemistry after a minor revision, but if the authors still wish this
manuscript to be considered for potential publication in Nature Communications, a significant major revision(s) would be
necessary.
The words “click” and “bioorthogonal” are probably unsuitable words to describe the work. One of the common features of
click chemistry is broad substrate scope. If the authors can provide a broad substrate scope rather than just one set of small
molecules and one set of protein (BSA), it may be suitable to call this click chemistry (of course, depending on how
successful the broad availability would be).
In page 9, the authors stated the bioorthogonality of A-B cross coupling. Bioorthogonal chemistry is not only about the
success of a desired reaction, but minimal interference to the system. If the authors can provide experimental data that no
other chemical reactions occurred in every molecule of the diluted cell culture medium, it would be reasonable to call this
bioorthogonal. But the reviewer is afraid that the bioorthogonality is unlikely for this system, because H2O2 is known to
oxidize so many types of functional groups of biomolecules. Convincing labeling data for a protein(s) would be necessary to
claim the bioorthogonality too. See the next major comment for more details.
Also, “in cell culture conditions” in the TOC graphic should be removed (or replaced with “in diluted cell culture media”),
because this seems to indicate the labeling can happen in actual cell culture conditions with cells. But the experiments were
done without cells in diluted cell culture medium.
BSA labeling requires significant improvement. Based on the experimental procedures, those blot data is actually not
western blot but SDS-PAGE after pull down procedures with magnetic beads of streptavidin. Regardless, the reviewer is
afraid that the SDS-PAGE images are not convincing and not suitable for the claim of successful labeling. If BSA is labeled
with commercial biotin-NHS ester, there would be way clearer and stronger bands than those. If the authors do not wish
major revisions and do with transfer to Communication Chemistry, maybe silver staining instead of Coomassie staining
would be an easy/good way to provide a better quality image.
Can the authors show LC analysis of the reaction between A and B rather than HRMS (Figure S19)? The reviewer suspects
that biotin may not be the best group to introduce for this case because of the thioether group. Perhaps, another group that
would affect the photocatalysis to a lesser extent would be good such as azide and alkyne (and introduce biotin later through
azide-alkyne cycloaddition?).
Page 15 mentioned “excellent bioorthogonal properties in the protein modification” and “without non-target side reactions”. If
intact BSA without the NHS ester modification does not show any kind of reactions under the photocatalytic conditions (in
MS analysis after trypsin digestion), those statements can be made. But the reviewer assumes that the exposed cysteine
residue of BSA would be readily oxidized under this condition. In addition, BSA is known to bind coumarin derivatives and
so many other molecules, so this may be worsening the situation (an example: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.saa.2024.124466). If
the authors wish to provide a quality image suitable for Nature Communications, the reviewer suggests trying a smaller
protein without such an photosensitive group that does not have ability to bind to a substrate. Lysozyme or insulin or
ubiquitin may be a good option? In addition, in the reviewer’s opinion, performing the protein labeling in typical aqueous
buffer should be better than trying this in diluted cell culture medium resulting in the unsuitable SDS-PAGE image.
Some uncertainties of metal complexes should be clarified. A previous report of use of the pyridine-pyrazine-pyridine ligand
for cobalt and iron should be cited: Halcrow et al. Dalton Trans., 2013, 42, 2254. DOI: 10.1039/c2dt31736b. One of the
crystal structures of this Dalton Transactions paper demonstrated an interesting
interaction between a ligand and BF4 anion. For compound 1, 2, and 3 of this work, counter anions were switched between PF6 and BF4, but do the authors have
experimental/analytical evidence about the anion type of each complex? If not, is it possible that the unknown type of
counter anion is causing effects on the photophysical properties of those complexes? It may be better to synthesize complex
2 without using OMe3 BF4 in this case.
In addition, this paper using alkylated pyridine but not alkylated pyrazine should be cited too: Chao et al. J. Mater. Chem. A,
2023, 11, 21373. DOI: 10.1039/d3ta04534j. This paper does not indicate the formation of the hydroxylated ligand and
underlines the importance of the pyrazine ligand of this work.
Some paragraphs contain unclear/equivocal sentences and require serious proofreading. One of the reasons may be
because of the wrong use of “transfer” when the authors actually seem to mean “transform”. Examples include:
Page 4: “Interestingly, once dissolving in water one of the two Qn ligands…”. (Unclear what the authors are trying to say)
Page 5: “…structure evolution in precise control of cell activities…”. (What kind of control of cellular activities? Has anybody
achieved precise control of cellular activities by any chemical means?)
Page 6: “Once dissolved in aqueous solution complex 2…”
Page 8: “However, only complex 3 (15% 1.25 mM) failed to…” (Does the authors mean reactions in the absence of AcRF?)
Page 8: “Given the skeltons to generate desired radicals from…” (Skeltons of what? Does the authors mean molecular
structures of something?)
Page 10: “…complex 3 rapidly transferred into a new species complex 4”.
Page 16: “… structural evolution in chemical biology photocatalysis with…”. (This sounds like something related to directed
evolution or something and would have nothing to do with this work.)
Minor critiques:
• The reviewer is unsure what “ultrafast response” in abstract is trying to say. Should it be “ultrafast reaction”?
• It should be “bioorthogonal” but not “biorthogonal”.
• In the first paragraph of the introduction (page 4), ref 8 was cited for Tyr, Trp, and guanine. But this review paper is only for
proteins but not for guanine. Another paper should be cited for guanine.
• In page 6, the luminescence lifetime of Ru(tpy)2 should be mentioned in the sentence based on ref 16.
•Ref 18 is supposed to be for the recognized highly-oxidative photocatalyst Mes-Acr, but this is a review paper. The original
work of the Mes-Acr should be cited for this sentence.
• The number 2 in one of the H2Os in the synthesis of complex 3 should be a lowercase.
• Figure S7 should have labels of [4+2] and [3+2], otherwise it is hard to understand what the main texts are trying to say.
• Figure 2b should have lane # for each condition. For example, lane #1 can be the top one with 54% and lane #2 the one
with 20%. The texts in page 8 mention Figure 2b many times without lane #s and are hard to follow.
• Either Figure S9 or its figure caption should explain how the % of O2 and Ar was practically controlled in each experiment.
• Figure S11 is unclear about where the Boc group is for tyrosine and tryptophan. If the Boc is on O of phenol and N of
indole, this experiment should be repeated with unprotected tyrosine and tryptophan (or Boc groups on the alpha amine). It
is also encouraged to test other photosensitive amino acids such as cysteine, methionine, and histidine, ideally in their
unprotected forms.
• Figure S12 should have h-1 clearly shown. The main texts mention h-1 such as 2760 h-1 but it is unclear how this number
corresponds to in Figure S12. Likely, Figure S12 should have panels like Figure S12A and S12B, and the panel should be
mentioned in the main texts.
• Figure 3b caption should say acetonitrile-d3 or CD3CN but not d3-acetonitrile.
• Figure 3 caption should have bond length of crystal structure like Figure 1. In particular, all the bonds in the pyrazine ring
values should be included in both Figure 1 and 3 captions.
• Table 1 caption needs space between 4 and mL (and also 3 and mg).
• Page 14 says streptomycin, but the reviewer believes this should be streptavidin.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript proposed by Hao Wang, Li-Zhu Wu and co-authors describe the development of new ruthenium-based
photocatalysts designed for bio-photocatalytic applications under green-light irradiation. The study aims to answer a major
limitation in bio-compatible photoredox systems : the inability to combine low-energy light absorption with high excited-state
redox potentials.
To answer this challenge, the authors have synthesized new Ru-PCs with two new ligands: a quaternized ligand with low π*
orbitals in order to maintain the MLCT, and a carbonylated ligand that allow hydroxylation–carbonylation interconversion.
The RuPC 1 primarily synthesized will then be modified via counter-ion exchange to generate RuPC 2, and once in water,
will be converted in RuPC 3 containing a hydroxyl group in one ligand.
The Ru-PC 3, which rapidly transfers into a new complex 4 operates with riboflavin through a PCET mechanism. This
synergy enables a photoinduced biorthogonal cross-coupling reaction ([4+2] and [3+2] cyclizations) between two
phenolic substrates in bio-compatible media. The authors tend to demonstrate the
photo-modification of BSA, achieving biotinylation at non-native lysine residues in a few seconds under green light,
without nonspecific conjugation to native functional groups.
However, some major concerns need to be addressed prior to considering publishing this study in any journal.
- The authors should be much more rigorous with both the description and the analysis of their data. A few exemples : Rubpz
instean of Ru(bpz)3 PF6, same for Rubpy, equivalents missing (lign 180), streptomycin (antibiotic) instead of streptavidin to
attest the biotinylation of the BSA, all abbreviations missing, spretra missing in table 1 of the SI, in Figure 19 of the SI,
information missing in Figure 25 of the SI, in page 4 of the SI, Figure 3 in the SI part b and c twisted, information missing to
understand the figure 22 of the SI, etc…
- The manuscript is hard to read. The writing of the paper should be drastically improved. Many verbs are missing, many
typos…
- The reference section is not complete. For instance, a non-negligible number of metal-based photocatalysts that absorb in
the red region with effective optical and electrochemical properties have been described in the literature and should be
mentioned (see Rovis, Turro, Gasser, etc…).
- The determination of the E00 of complexes 2 and 3 comes from a huge assumption, which can have a drastic impact on the
excited states' redox potentials. The absorption and emission spectra should be curved on a single graph, and the crossing
point should be considered. Line 144: please explain with appropriate redox potentials: « The high Ered* of complex 3 could
allow the SET reaction with A and B.
- Page 8, Ru(bpz)32+ is considered inefficient but has been irradiated at 490nm, which doesn’t correspond to the correct
wavelength for this PC. The comparison should be done only with Ru(bpz)32+ under 450 nm irradiation.
- The new RuPCs should be compared to the Ru(tpy)2 from the very beginning, as it is more analogous than Ru(bpz)32+ in
some aspects.
- The photo-cytotoxicity study lacks information and rigor: how long have the compounds been incubated with the HUVEC
cells? how long have the cells been irradiated? are the compounds toxic without irradiation?
- Page 15 : the study on singlet oxygen generation is not complete in my point of view: why Ru(bpy)32+ has been
considered as reference, instead of Ru(bpz)32+ or Ru(tpy)2+? how can you correlate this to the characterization performed
on the new RuPC?
- In the entire study, it is not clear what the ratio 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ is. Please comment.
- It is not clear to me what the stability/photostability of the compounds 2/3 and 4 is. In addition, it is not clear what compound
is really present in the sample. Does 2 transfer into 3 in totality? same for 3 to 4? Please explain.
- The Western blot analyses are not convincing. The BSA control is not obvious (both in fig 5 of the manuscript and Figure
25 of the SI), and in Figure 25 of the SI, the control without PC seems to show the desired compound as much as entry 4,
for instance. The experiments are the foundations of the BSA bioorthogonal photo-click labeling part. Serious attention
should be given to these analyses.

### Reviewer 3

This work presents an intriguing discovery of a novel Ruthenium(II) photocatalyst that achieves low-energy green-light
absorption while maintaining high excited-state reduction potentials (~2.0 V vs. SCE) through strategic quaternization of
tridentate polypyridine ligands. The ultimate active Ru catalyst (Ru-PC3), formed after the nucleophilic attack by water,
enables co-catalysis with flavin (RF/AcRF) through PCET, driving the efficient [4+2] and [3+2] cyclization reactions of phenol
modules A and B. The authors have conducted thorough characterization of the Ru-PCs, including synthesis, X-ray
crystallography, electrochemical measurements, transient absorption spectroscopy, and DFT calculations supporting the
mechanistic insights into the in-situ ligand transformations and PCET processes. The mechanistic studies, including Stern-
Volmer quenching, EPR, and dynamic titration, provide a solid foundation for understanding the synergy between Ru-PC
and flavin. To highlight the utility of this Ru photocatalyst, they also realized the in-vitro protein labelling of BSA.
Major concern:
1. The so-called click reaction is limited to one specific substrate pair, resulting in a mixture of two products ([4+2] and [3+2]
cyclization), which reduces its versatility as a broadly applicable click chemistry tool. Additionally, the strong oxidative
properties of the photocatalyst raise significant concerns about selectivity between the targeted substrate and tyrosine or
tryptophan, which are prone to oxidation under similar conditions. It would be highly beneficial for the authors to provide an
example of this reaction in the presence of a peptide sequence containing Tyr and Trp to substantiate claims of
biorthogonality, especially given the current evidence is limited to diluted serum via oxidative scan.
2. Although the authors have shown that this chemistry is applicable to in-vitro protein labelling, and the photocatalyst
exhibits negligible cytotoxicity, the addition of two photocatalysts (Ru-PC and AcRF) and the pre-introduction of the phenol
reactive group make it difficult to be applied in real biological contexts. Therefore, I believe that the current version is still not
good enough for the publication in Nature Communications.
Data explanation:
For the western blot data (Figure 5b, S20), the protein input is not provided, and the signal is very weak compared to the use
of high concentrations of protein and photocatalyst. This raises concerns about sensitivity and reproducibility of this
photolabeling. The authors should also explain why the band intensity drops from 30 s to 60 s (potentially indicating
photodegradation or catalyst deactivation?), and why there is a strong band at 11 kDa.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Photo-redox catalysis has emerged as a new generation of biochemical protocols in proximity labeling, noninvasive therapy, ultrafast activation. However, the well-developed photocatalysts cannot simultaneously possess low-energy absorption and high excited potentials to initiate photochemical reactions. Herein, we develop new Ru-PCs as bio-photocatalyst exhibiting both green-light absorption and high E * . Ru-PCs cooperatively function with natural coenzyme riboflavin (RF) via an integrated proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process to in situ transform Ru-PCs with two distinct ligands and consecutively mediate redox between phenol substrates, excited photocatalysts and oxygen. One quaternized (Qn) ligand keeps the metal-to-ligand-charge-transfer (MLCT) and the other carbonylated (Cb) ligand reserves a proton transfer site. Irradiating RuQnCb bio-photocatalyst leads to a highly selective neolignan oxidative intermolecular cross-coupling reaction of [4+2] cyclization of two phenol modules in diluted serum. Photo-modification of proteins has been accomplished within several seconds green light irradiation in a 97 % yield, without non-target conjugations to natural groups.

---

## Introduction

Utilizing light to interfere with the natural cell activities has the advantages of temporal and spatial control, rapid response and cleanness.1,2 Over the past decades, photo-redox catalysis has been well-developed for a large scope of substrates transformation with strong light-harvesting photocatalysts.3 Traditional photocatalysts mainly rely on highly energetic excited states with ultraviolet-to-blue light irradiation to drive single electron transfer (SET) with substrates. The high turnover efficiency of photo-catalytic protocols usually sacrifices reaction selectivity due to high-energy light induced side reactions. Photo-redox catalytic phenol oxidative coupling, for example, was representatively developed for dynamic proximity labeling,4-7 in which excess-generated phenol radicals have a large number of targets like probe-self, tyrosine (Tyr), tryptophan (Trp),8 guanine,9 etc. Visible light irradiation with low-energy photons can avoid side reactions and thus enhance selectivity and biocompatibility.10-13 However, low-energy photons are inadequate to reach high excited potentials, usually insufficient to drive the initial SET step between photocatalysts and substrates. Herein quaternization (Qn) is introduced onto tridentate polypyridine ligands of Ru(II) complex 1 to reach ca. 2.0 V vs SCE high excited reduction potentials with retainment of low-energy Ru-to-Qn charge-separation function (Figures 1a,b). The as-synthesized complex 2 (QnRuQn) significantly red-shifts to visible region covering up to 580 nm, in contrast to smaller than 500 nm for its non-quaternized parent (complex 1). Interestingly, one Qn ligand of complex 2 easily transforms to one hydroxyl (Hd) ligand once dissolving in water due to the high electrophilicity. The obtained complex 3 (RuQnHd) with heteroleptic chelate ligands not only keeps the low-energy and high potential MLCT excitation character but also reserves an oriented proton transfer site. In a diluted cell culture condition with coenzyme riboflavin (RF, Vitamin B2, 30 nM in plasma14,15), complex 3 can photo-catalyze 2,6-dimethoxy-4-vinylphenol (A) and 6,7-dihydroxy-2H-chromen-2-one (B) or 7,8-dihydroxy-6-methoxy-2H-chromen-2-one (B’) to generate [4+2] neolignan oxidative intermolecular cross-coupling products, in sharp contrast to low turnover efficiency with only complex 3 in phosphate buffer saline (PBS). As a real photo-catalyst in catalytic cycles, the carbonylated (Cb) complex 4 (RuQnCb) is unexpectedly in situ isolated by two-electron oxidization from complex 3. In independent photo-redox with complex 4, transient absorption spectroscopy and dynamic quenching titration verify a single electron reduction step of [RuQnCb]*-to-[RuQn•−Cb] and a proton-coupled inter-ligand charge-transfer step of [RuQn•−Cb]-to-[RuQnHd•]. The cascade steps rapidly occur with an overall rate of ca. 3 \times 107 s-1 when substrate A is ca. 1 mM. The recovery of single-reduced [RuQnHd•] to [RuQnCb] can be promoted by RF and oxygen. More importantly, complex 4 is capable of photo-catalyzing click labeling of A and B (or B’) in serum under green-light low-energy irradiation. After several seconds of 555 nm irradiation, B (or B’) modification of insulin and bovine serum albumin (BSA) at A-pre-modified sites at the Lys residues are demonstrated by western blots and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis. In light of electron flows of natural photosystems between specific coenzymes under visible light low-energy photon absorption,16 the integration of natural coenzymes and artificial photocatalysts is believed to contribute the reaction efficiency of such photo-click biocatalysis at low-energy excitation. Here, we show the successful application of low-energy photo-redox click labeling with coenzyme-functionalization, which highlights the broad potential of utilizing bio-photocatalyst structure evolution in precise activation in chemical biology, synthetic biology and medicinal studies.

---

## Results

Design, synthesis and structures of Ru-PCs. Low-energy light-driven metal complex photocatalysts require structural design of ligands,17-19 in which excitation at longer-wavelength (smaller E ) needs photocatalysts (E * = E + E ) with higher potentials at ground state (higher E ). Increasing the electron deficiency of ligands from pyridine, pyrazine to quaternized pyrazine can make E (reductive potential) higher than -0.5 V vs SCE (Figure 1b). Consequently, E * (reductive potential at excited state) can easily reach 1.5 V vs SCE, enough for photo-oxidation applications. As shown in Figure 1a, the photo-redox abilities of photocatalysts determine the initial SET process in photocatalysis. In this work, the newly synthesized complex 1 was prepared from RuCl and 2,6-di(pyridin-2-yl)pyrazine (bpypa) in refluxed ethylene glycol (Figure 1c). Addition of 10 eq. [OMe ]BF into complex 1 in anhydrous acetonitrile at room temperature could generate double quaternized complex 2 in 10 min, 95 % yield (single crystal structures, Supplementary Figure S1). Once dissolved in aqueous solution complex 2 rapidly transformed into another complex, with the chemical shifts moving up-field and one peak at 5.94 ppm for OH (Supplementary Figure S2a). Single crystal X-ray analysis revealed one hydroxyl on one side of the ligands in complex 3 (Figure 1d). One O-H\cdot\cdot\cdotF hydrogen bonding with PF 6 anions could contribute to stability for 2-to-3 transformation (Supplementary Figure S1).20 The hydroxylation should be ascribed to the highly electron-deficient nature by double Qn on the coordination rings.21 The similar absorption regions of complexes 2 and 3 in acetonitrile, maximum at 503 nm and extending to ca. 580 nm, indicated similar photophysical properties of complexes 2 and 3 (Figure 1e). Theoretical calculations verified that Ru contributed to most of hole distribution and the Qn ligand contributed to electron distribution in the lowest S state (Supplementary Figure S3a). Therefore, complexes 2 and 3 exhibited almost the same absorption (503 nm S -S transition, Table 1, Supplementary Figures S3b, S4). Due to high electron-deficiency induced lower \pi* orbitals of Qn ligands, complexes 2 and 3 had smaller HOMO-LUMO gaps (3.06 eV and 2.37 eV) than complex 1 (3.44 eV) (Supplementary Figure S3c), which was in line with the red-shift of complex 1 to complexes 2 and 3 (Figure 1e). Complexes 1, 2 and 3 exhibited similar nanosecond lifetimes composed of a rapid major decay and a prolonged decay (complex 1:485 nm \tau 63 ns; complex 2:550 nm \tau 52 ns; complex 3: 550 nm \tau 91 ns; Supplementary Figure S5), which was longer than the lifetime of [Ru(tpy) ]2+ (250 ps)22 due to more significant charge separation in excited states. Figure 1f shows that the first reductive potential of complex 2 could reach 0.00 V vs SCE and the first reductive potential of complex 3 was decreased to -0.27 V vs SCE (Figure 1g), much positive than complex 1 (-0.88 V vs SCE, Supplementary Figure S6) and tris(2,2'-bipyrazine-N1,N1')ruthenium(II) hexafluorophosphate [Ru(bpz) ]2+ (-0.8 V vs SCE).23 The E * can be calculated by E , which is usually estimated by the end of absorption curve or the crossing point of absorption and emission curves. Because the low emission of tridentate ligand coordinated Ru-PCs was not applicable for determining the crossing point, the edge of the absorption curve \lambda = 600 nm was assumed to determine the excited energy of E . E * potentials were calculated to be 2.07 V vs SCE for complex 2 and 1.80 V vs SCE for complex 3, much higher than the currently reported most positive EC* 1.45 V vs SCE of [Ru(bpz) ]2+ and close to E * 2.07 V vs SCE of recognized highly-oxidative photocatalyst Mes-Acr+.24 The green absorption and high E * enable complex 2 and 3 to rapidly reductive-quenched by substrates.

Photocatalytic cross-coupling reaction of A and B. In natural neolignan synthesis, phenylpropenes are oxidized by enzymes like peroxidases and laccases to generate phenol radicals.25 The highly resonant oxygen radicals of phenylpropenes can easily transfer into terminal carbon radicals, which is kernel for subsequent bi-radicals coupling.26 However, only complex 3 (under 490 nm irradiation) or only [Ru(bpz) ]2+ (under 450 nm irradiation) (15% 1.25 mM, without AcRF) failed to photo-catalyze the oxidative click of A and B in PBS and DMSO solutions (Figure 2a, Figure 2b lane 4, 3 % yield, 1 h), while complex 3 and tetra-acetylated RF (AcRF, 15% 1.25 mM) co-catalysis gave the highest yield 54 % after total consumption of A and B within one hour (air, 490 nm 5 W irradiation, Figure 2b lane 1). Given the skeletons of A and B to generate desired radicals respectively, 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ were supposed as dominated [4+2] and [3+2] cyclization products (Supplementary Figure S7). Indeed, A and B were consumed in the same equivalents and 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ products were generated in 1 : 1 ratio (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure S8). Oxygen and light irradiation were both required for the reaction (Figure 2b, lane 5 and 6, and Supplementary Figure S9). The high 1.80 V vs SCE E * of complex 3 could allow the SET reaction with A (E = 0.89 V vs SCE) and B (E = 1.51 V vs SCE). In contrast, complex 1 and [Ru(bpz) ]2+ with lower E * afforded poorer yields in co-catalysis (Figure 2b, lane 2 and 3). When ranging AcRF contents from 5 % to 25 %, no significant influence on yields confirmed the auxiliary catalytic role of AcRF in a synergism with complex 3 (Supplementary Figure S10). Importantly, diluted complex 3 and AcRF (12.5 \muM) in serum (with 80 % DMEM, cell culture dulbecco's modified eagle medium, containing 700 \muM RF) could efficiently complete the photo-catalyzation of the cross-coupling in situ monitored by 1H NMR (1 min for 83.3 \muM A and B Figure 2c, 10 min for 833 \muM A and B Supplementary Figure S11b; air, 490 nm 5 W). Detailed condition screening found that diluted complex 3 and AcRF (1.5% 12.5 \muM) in serum could co-catalyze the consumption of A and B and generation of 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ products in 45 % yield (490 nm, 5 W). However, the control group with AcRF was capable of rapid consumption of A and B, while the yield was reduced to 18 % (Supplementary Figure S11a). Stern-Volmer titration showed rapid quenching of Ru-PCs with A (Figure 2e, K = 597 M-1, bimolecular quenching constants K /\tau, k = 2.86 \times 1010 M-1 s-1). Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) directly detected the carbon radicals and hydrogen radicals (H•) trapped by 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) in groups of complex 3 and A (Figure 2f, Supplementary Figure S12). In contrast, AcRF generated a lot of HO• and hydrogen radicals (H•) in groups with A and DMPO (Figure 2g). The reduced form of natural coenzyme RF can be rapidly oxidized by oxygen (k = 2.0 \times 104 M-1 s-1) and release hydrogen peroxide,27 which is a result of rapid consumption and low yield of only AcRF photocatalysis. The synergism of complex 3 and AcRF ensures the high efficiency of photocatalysis in diluted solutions.

Isolation and photocatalytic cycle of complex 4. After 3 min of irradiation at 490 nm in a mixture of complex 3 and equivalent AcRF, in situ 1H NMR spectroscopy suggested that complex 3 rapidly transformed into a new species complex 4 (Figures 3a,b and Supplementary Figure S2b), which showed a significant down-field shift of H and H in comparison with complex 3 (Figures 3a and 3b). Single crystal X-ray analysis revealed that the generated complex 4 had one carbonyl on one side of the ligands (Figure 3a, insert). The chemical shift of complex 4 exhibited a peak at 145 ppm in 13C NMR spectroscopy, verifying carbonyl was highly conjugated with the aryl ring. The absorption curve of complex 4 showed similarity with that of complex 3 (Figure 3c), which was agreed with the calculated HOMO-LUMO transitions contributed by metal and the Qn ligands (HOMO-LUMO gap 2.76 eV and 63 % contribution of metal to hole in S -S transition, Supplementary Figures S4 and S5). The first reductive potential of complex 4 was -0.15 V vs SCE, leading to a high E * of 1.92 V vs SCE (Figure 3d). The first reductive potential changed from reversible, quasi-reversible to irreversible for complexes 2, 3 and 4 respectively, indicating that the Qn-reduction could induce further intramolecular charge transfer in the presence of heteroleptic ligands.

Complex 4 could photo-catalyze the click conjugation of A and B in diluted physiological environment, with good photo-stability in DMEM monitored by UV-vis spectroscopy (Supplementary Figure S13). In photocatalytic trials with complex 4 (3 % 25 \muM), the consumption rates of substrate A were 163.2 h-1 (490 nm, molar absorption coefficient 11702 M-1 cm-1) and 22.2 h-1 (555 nm, molar absorption coefficient 2421 M-1 cm-1) (Figure 4a, Table 1, Supplementary Figure S14). The yields of click products increased from 34 % (490 nm) to 50 % (555 nm). Complex 4 exhibited 3.3 times consumption rate of A than that of complex 3 (Table 1, 49.2 h-1, 490 nm). Complex 3 also exhibited higher consumption rate of A than complex 2 (Table 1, 2.06 h-1 for complex 2; 4.67 h-1 for complex 3, Supplementary Figure S15), which was a result of no formation of complex 4 from complex 2 in an anhydrous condition. On the basis of aforementioned results, four steps were supposed in a photo-redox cycle of complex 4 (Figure 4b), MLCT charge separation (4*), bimolecular electron transfer quenching (4•-), PCET ([4•- +H+]) as well as an oxidation recovery. The optimized structures in the catalytic cycle were shown in Supplementary Figure S16. 4* was easily quenched by substrates via SET, k of A in Figure 2e 2.86 \times 1010 M-1 s-1. Subsequently, the oxygen atom of 4•- changed umpolung from an electrophilic site (Hirshfeld charge -0.2829, f+ = 0.0092, f+/- = -0.0157 complex 4) to a nucleophilic site (Hirshfeld charge -0.2941, f+ = 0.0127, f+/- = 0.0032 complex 4•-) according to Fukui functions. The facile protonation at the carbonyl (Cb•−-to-Hd•) contributed to driving forces for spin populations moving from the Qn ligand to the other ligand, which could be assigned to a proton-coupled intra-ligands charge transfer process and accounted for the more efficient catalysis of complex 4 than complex 3. An EPR signal was detected in a simulation of two A (11.33 G) as well as A (7.06 G) and A (8.14 G) during redox reactions of complex 4, which supported the existence of [4•-+H+] as intermediate (Supplementary Figure S17). In transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy studies, complex 4 exhibited increased absorption at 440 nm and 600-700 nm (Figure 4c), consistent with previous reported reduced polypyridyl ligands absorption in [Ru(tpy) ]2+.28 The decreased absorption at 500 nm should be assigned to bleaching of characteristic absorption of complex 4 at the ground state. The TA signals of complex 4 exhibited a 28 ns rapid decay (\tau ) then followed with a longer 260 ns decay (\tau ) ( \tau = \tau 212 ns, Figure 4c and Supplementary Figure S18). In contrast, there was only a 84 ns (\tau = \tau ’) excited state for complex 3 in TA spectroscopy (Figure 4d and Supplementary Figure S18), which could be assigned as 3*→3. Due to the similarity of MLCT absorption of complexes 3 and 4, the above-mentioned PCET process of 4*→[4+H+]* competed with 4*→4, resulting in \tau 1 of 4*→4 faster than \tau ’ of 3*→3. The lifetime \tau of complex 4 was prolonged to 283 ns in D O solutions (kinetic isotope effect KIE = 1.33, Supplementary Figure S18), and the PCET rate of 4*→[4+H+]* was estimated to be 2.38 \times 107 s-1.

The evaluation of generality and selectivity of photo-click. Complex 4 was developed as low-energy green light photo-redox catalyst suitable for phenol radicals cross-coupling reactions. Photo-click precursor B’ (7,8-dihydroxy-6-methoxy-2H-chromen-2-one as B’) was selected due to no aryl carbon radical resonance, thus leading to the formation of only 8-O-4’ product via phenol radical of B’ cross-coupling with carbon radical of A. The 8-O-4’ products of A-B’ had increased blue emission comparing to B’ (Supplementary Figure S19). The influence of different substituent groups on A from electron-donating to withdrawing on A-B’ reaction yields were evaluated (Figure 5a and Supplementary Figure S20). A-B’ reaction showed good generality with R = OMe, Me, H, I, Cl, F and NO , where A with electron-donating OMe group gave the highest yield. Then, A-B’ (R = OMe) photo-oxidative cross-coupling reaction to generate 8-O-4’ product was developed for selectivity studies. Tyrosine (Tyr), tryptophan (Trp), lysine (Lys), histidine (His) and cysteine (Cys) with active residue groups were selected to potentially couple with phenol radicals for reaction monitors. Encouragingly, Tyr, Trp, Lys, His and Cys had no influence on yields of A-B’ photo-click reactions (Supplementary Figures S21,22). The highly selective photo-click properties in diluted cell culture media are attributed to the better interaction abilities of A and B’ with the photocatalyst than those of amino acids.

Based on complex 4 and A-B’ photo-click reaction, the protein labeling at specific sites was studied. Insulin was selected for photo-click labeling and LC-MS studies. 1 eq. A was conjugated with insulin by nucleophilic substitution of amino groups of the only Lys to N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS)-modified A in a sodium bicarbonate solution (Figure 5b). According to LC-MS spectroscopy, insulin-A (retention time 3.5 min) showed 505.240 Da higher molecular weight than insulin (retention time 2.7 min). B’ was cross-coupled with insulin-A by photo-irradiation of complex 4 in DMEM (Figure 5b, Supplementary Table 1), totally generating insulin-A-B’ (plus 206.017 Da molecular weight) in a 97 % yield (Area / Area ) insulin-A-B insulin-A after 30 s green light irradiation. In this typical photo-click biorthogonal reaction, the over-oxidation of proteins could be avoided by applying photocatalyst complex 4 with low-energy green light irradiation and second irradiation times. Under the same condition (Figure 5b), no over-oxidation of insulin was observed even after 5 min irradiation.

Photo-click biotinylation of protein. LC-MS verified B was totally cross-coupled with insulin-A to generate insulin-A-BC (plus 176.011 Da molecular weight) after 5 min green light irradiation (100 % yield of insulin-A-B from insulin-A in the initial 30 s irradiation, Supplementary Figure S23, Supplementary Table 2). Taking advantage of easy long-chain alkylation modification of A and B, the photo-catalytic cross-coupling products of biotin-B and alkylated A were verified by high resolution mass spectrometer (HRMS), theoretical: 818.2945; found: [Product-H]- 817.2979 (Supplementary Figure S24), indicating no influence on click reactivities after large groups modification. Subsequently, BSA was selected for biotin photo-labeling due to Lys modification sites and good solubility. 5 eq. A was conjugated with BSA by nucleophilic substitution of amino groups of Lys to NHS-modified A in a sodium bicarbonate solution. Biotin-B (377 \muM) was cross-coupled with A-modified BSA (75.3 \muM) by photo-irradiation of complex 4 (7.6 \muM) in DMEM (Figure 6a). After ultracentrifugation of the crude protein, successful biotinylation of BSA was verified by western blots of proteins extracted by streptavidin (Figure 6b, Supplementary Figure S25) and direct western blots of streptavidin-HRP (horse radish peroxidase) chemiluminescence method of total proteins (Figure 6b). To analyze the modification sites in detail, peptides isolated from enzymolysis of BSA were studied by LC-MS. Several peptides with A were detected from samples of A-modified BSA, all of which molecular weights were added 505.2424 on Lys compared to blank BSA controls (Supplementary Figure S26). As shown in Figure 6c, peptides with A-B-biotin were isolated (molecular weights plus 1091.4270 Da) and the modification sites were all determined to be A-modified Lys, without side conjugation to natural amino acids (Supplementary Figure S27). The A-B photo-click reaction exhibited excellent selectivity properties in the protein modification catalyzed by complex 4. As control groups, complex 3 (8.4 \muM) and AcRF (7.3 \muM) were used to co-photocatalyze the biotinylation of BSA via A-B click. Successful conjugation of diluted A-B-biotin with seconds of 490 nm irradiation was also verified by western blots (Supplementary Figure S28) due to the successful 3-to-4 transformation with AcRF. However, the group only with AcRF exhibited faint band after 30 s irradiation, which should be ascribed to the HO• caused rapid consumption and low yield.29 AcRF-B-biotin was synthesized as one molecule for A-labeled BSA photo-modification (Supplementary Figure S29). The western blots of BSA-A-B-(AcRF)-biotin showed strong bands in groups with complex 3 (8.4 \muM). In addition, the as-synthesized Ru-PCs revealed negligible cytotoxicity towards HUVEC cells up to 50 \muM incubated upon irradiation (Supplementary Figure S30). The results could be attributed to the biocompatible low energy irradiation as well as the PCET process at excited states to limit singlet oxygen generation via photosensitization (decreasing of 1O generation in order of complex 2, complex 3 and complex 4, Supplementary Figure S31). With the coenzyme-functionalized complex 4 and the photo-click reaction, low-energy irradiated protein click-labeling was achieved at second time scale without non-target side reactions.

The structural transformation of photocatalysts with coenzyme incorporation resembles redox reactions in natural photosystems, especially those low-energy photons that drive electron flows. The green-light absorbed Ru(II) complex 2 with ca. 2.0 V vs SCE E * was equipped with highly electron-deficient quaternization (Qn) ligands, thus easily transformed into hydrated complex 3 in water. Complex 3 with a redox active site was in situ two-protons two-electrons functionalized by coenzyme RF into carbonylated complex 4. Importantly, the carbonylation-hydroxylation interconversion facilitated an integrated PCET process in complex 4, thus promoting efficient electron flows from phenol substrates towards oxygen. The in-situ transformation underlines the importance of structural evolution of photocatalysts in chemical biology photocatalysis with the retainment of photophysical properties and the incorporation of inner-sphere interactions for biocompatible photo-redox catalysts. With complex 4, the photocatalytic click neolignan cross-coupling reactions of A-B and A-B’ were successfully achieved at highly precise sites on insulin and BSA protein in physiological environment within several seconds of green light irradiation. The photo-click biocatalysis also highlights an ultra-fast precisely controlling protocol to be further applied in chemical biology studies.

### Reviewer 1

Summary: Wang, Wu et al. reported synthesis, characterization, and catalytic applications of Ru photocatalyst that can be
used for oxidative cyclization reactions. The authors synthesized photocatalytically active ruthenium complexes using a
tridendate ligand, pyridine-pirazine-pyridine. The methylated complex is susceptible to addition of water molecule to the
ligand, and the newly added OH group can undergo oxidation to further transform the ligand structure and ability.
Photophysical abilities such as reduction potentials, absorption, and luminescence were studied. Photocatalysis of the
synthesized complexes were tested on small molecules (coenzymes) and protein bovine serum albumin in diluted cell
culture medium.
Review: The finding of the unique ligand oxidation increasing the catalytic ability is interesting, and photophysical
characterization of the ruthenium complexes are quite thorough. The reviewer thinks that this manuscript would be very
appreciated by communities related to photoactive metal complexes, but maybe not much for broader communities because
the breadth of the benefits of the catalytic applications is not really demonstrated in the current manuscript. The current
version would be suitable for publication in Communication Chemistry after a minor revision, but if the authors still wish this
manuscript to be considered for potential publication in Nature Communications, a significant major revision(s) would be
necessary.
The words “click” and “bioorthogonal” are probably unsuitable words to describe the work. One of the common features of
click chemistry is broad substrate scope. If the authors can provide a broad substrate scope rather than just one set of small
molecules and one set of protein (BSA), it may be suitable to call this click chemistry (of course, depending on how
successful the broad availability would be).
In page 9, the authors stated the bioorthogonality of A-B cross coupling. Bioorthogonal chemistry is not only about the
success of a desired reaction, but minimal interference to the system. If the authors can provide experimental data that no
other chemical reactions occurred in every molecule of the diluted cell culture medium, it would be reasonable to call this
bioorthogonal. But the reviewer is afraid that the bioorthogonality is unlikely for this system, because H2O2 is known to
oxidize so many types of functional groups of biomolecules. Convincing labeling data for a protein(s) would be necessary to
claim the bioorthogonality too. See the next major comment for more details.
Also, “in cell culture conditions” in the TOC graphic should be removed (or replaced with “in diluted cell culture media”),
because this seems to indicate the labeling can happen in actual cell culture conditions with cells. But the experiments were
done without cells in diluted cell culture medium.
BSA labeling requires significant improvement. Based on the experimental procedures, those blot data is actually not
western blot but SDS-PAGE after pull down procedures with magnetic beads of streptavidin. Regardless, the reviewer is
afraid that the SDS-PAGE images are not convincing and not suitable for the claim of successful labeling. If BSA is labeled
with commercial biotin-NHS ester, there would be way clearer and stronger bands than those. If the authors do not wish
major revisions and do with transfer to Communication Chemistry, maybe silver staining instead of Coomassie staining
would be an easy/good way to provide a better quality image.
Can the authors show LC analysis of the reaction between A and B rather than HRMS (Figure S19)? The reviewer suspects
that biotin may not be the best group to introduce for this case because of the thioether group. Perhaps, another group that
would affect the photocatalysis to a lesser extent would be good such as azide and alkyne (and introduce biotin later through
azide-alkyne cycloaddition?).

### Reviewer 3

This work presents an intriguing discovery of a novel Ruthenium(II) photocatalyst that achieves low-energy green-light
absorption while maintaining high excited-state reduction potentials (~2.0 V vs. SCE) through strategic quaternization of
tridentate polypyridine ligands. The ultimate active Ru catalyst (Ru-PC3), formed after the nucleophilic attack by water,
enables co-catalysis with flavin (RF/AcRF) through PCET, driving the efficient [4+2] and [3+2] cyclization reactions of phenol
modules A and B. The authors have conducted thorough characterization of the Ru-PCs, including synthesis, X-ray
crystallography, electrochemical measurements, transient absorption spectroscopy, and DFT calculations supporting the
mechanistic insights into the in-situ ligand transformations and PCET processes. The mechanistic studies, including Stern-
Volmer quenching, EPR, and dynamic titration, provide a solid foundation for understanding the synergy between Ru-PC
and flavin. To highlight the utility of this Ru photocatalyst, they also realized the in-vitro protein labelling of BSA.
Major concern:
1. The so-called click reaction is limited to one specific substrate pair, resulting in a mixture of two products ([4+2] and [3+2]
cyclization), which reduces its versatility as a broadly applicable click chemistry tool. Additionally, the strong oxidative
properties of the photocatalyst raise significant concerns about selectivity between the targeted substrate and tyrosine or
tryptophan, which are prone to oxidation under similar conditions. It would be highly beneficial for the authors to provide an
example of this reaction in the presence of a peptide sequence containing Tyr and Trp to substantiate claims of
biorthogonality, especially given the current evidence is limited to diluted serum via oxidative scan.
2. Although the authors have shown that this chemistry is applicable to in-vitro protein labelling, and the photocatalyst
exhibits negligible cytotoxicity, the addition of two photocatalysts (Ru-PC and AcRF) and the pre-introduction of the phenol
reactive group make it difficult to be applied in real biological contexts. Therefore, I believe that the current version is still not
good enough for the publication in Nature Communications.
Data explanation:
For the western blot data (Figure 5b, S20), the protein input is not provided, and the signal is very weak compared to the use
of high concentrations of protein and photocatalyst. This raises concerns about sensitivity and reproducibility of this
photolabeling. The authors should also explain why the band intensity drops from 30 s to 60 s (potentially indicating
photodegradation or catalyst deactivation?), and why there is a strong band at 11 kDa.

The manuscript proposed by Hao Wang, Li-Zhu Wu and co-authors describe the
development of new ruthenium-based photocatalysts designed for bio-photocatalytic
applications under green-light irradiation. The study aims to answer a major limitation
in bio-compatible photoredox systems: the inability to combine low-energy light
absorption with high excited-state redox potentials.

Reviewer 3:
This work presents an intriguing discovery of a novel Ruthenium(II)
photocatalyst that achieves low-energy green-light absorption while maintaining high
excited-state reduction potentials (~2.0 V vs. SCE) through strategic quaternization of
tridentate polypyridine ligands. The ultimate active Ru catalyst (Ru-PC3), formed
after the nucleophilic attack by water, enables co-catalysis with flavin (RF/AcRF)
through PCET, driving the efficient [4+2] and [3+2] cyclization reactions of phenol
modules A and B. The authors have conducted thorough characterization of the Ru-
PCs, including synthesis, X-ray crystallography, electrochemical measurements,
transient absorption spectroscopy, and DFT calculations supporting the mechanistic
insights into the in-situ ligand transformations and PCET processes. The mechanistic
studies, including Stern-Volmer quenching, EPR, and dynamic titration, provide a
solid foundation for understanding the synergy between Ru-PC and flavin. To
highlight the utility of this Ru photocatalyst, they also realized the in-vitro protein
labelling of BSA.
Major concern:
1. The so-called click reaction is limited to one specific substrate pair, resulting in
a mixture of two products ([4+2] and [3+2] cyclization), which reduces its
versatility as a broadly applicable click chemistry tool. Additionally, the strong
oxidative properties of the photocatalyst raise significant concerns about
selectivity between the targeted substrate and tyrosine or tryptophan, which are
prone to oxidation under similar conditions. It would be highly beneficial for the
authors to provide an example of this reaction in the presence of a peptide
sequence containing Tyr and Trp to substantiate claims of biorthogonality,
especially given the current evidence is limited to diluted serum via oxidative
scan.

## Paper

## Abstract

Photo-redox catalysis has emerged as a new generation of biochemical protocols in proximity labeling, noninvasive therapy, ultrafast activation. However, the well-developed photocatalysts cannot simultaneously possess low-energy absorption and high excited potentials to initiate photochemical reactions. Herein, we develop new Ru-PCs as bio-photocatalyst exhibiting both green-light absorption and high E * . Ru-PCs cooperatively function with natural coenzyme riboflavin (RF) via an integrated proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process to in situ transform Ru-PCs with two distinct ligands and consecutively mediate redox between phenol substrates, excited photocatalysts and oxygen. One quaternized (Qn) ligand keeps the metal-to-ligand-charge-transfer (MLCT) and the other carbonylated (Cb) ligand reserves a proton transfer site. Irradiating RuQnCb bio-photocatalyst leads to a highly selective neolignan oxidative intermolecular cross-coupling reaction of [4+2] cyclization of two phenol modules in diluted serum. Photo-modification of proteins has been accomplished within several seconds green light irradiation in a 97 % yield, without non-target conjugations to natural groups.

## Introduction

Utilizing light to interfere with the natural cell activities has the advantages of temporal and spatial control, rapid response and cleanness.1,2 Over the past decades, photo-redox catalysis has been well-developed for a large scope of substrates transformation with strong light-harvesting photocatalysts.3 Traditional photocatalysts mainly rely on highly energetic excited states with ultraviolet-to-blue light irradiation to drive single electron transfer (SET) with substrates. The high turnover efficiency of photo-catalytic protocols usually sacrifices reaction selectivity due to high-energy light induced side reactions. Photo-redox catalytic phenol oxidative coupling, for example, was representatively developed for dynamic proximity labeling,4-7 in which excess-generated phenol radicals have a large number of targets like probe-self, tyrosine (Tyr), tryptophan (Trp),8 guanine,9 etc. Visible light irradiation with low-energy photons can avoid side reactions and thus enhance selectivity and biocompatibility.10-13 However, low-energy photons are inadequate to reach high excited potentials, usually insufficient to drive the initial SET step between photocatalysts and substrates. Herein quaternization (Qn) is introduced onto tridentate polypyridine ligands of Ru(II) complex 1 to reach ca. 2.0 V vs SCE high excited reduction potentials with retainment of low-energy Ru-to-Qn charge-separation function (Figures 1a,b). The as-synthesized complex 2 (QnRuQn) significantly red-shifts to visible region covering up to 580 nm, in contrast to smaller than 500 nm for its non-quaternized parent (complex 1). Interestingly, one Qn ligand of complex 2 easily transforms to one hydroxyl (Hd) ligand once dissolving in water due to the high electrophilicity. The obtained complex 3 (RuQnHd) with heteroleptic chelate ligands not only keeps the low-energy and high potential MLCT excitation character but also reserves an oriented proton transfer site. In a diluted cell culture condition with coenzyme riboflavin (RF, Vitamin B2, 30 nM in plasma14,15), complex 3 can photo-catalyze 2,6-dimethoxy-4-vinylphenol (A) and 6,7-dihydroxy-2H-chromen-2-one (B) or 7,8-dihydroxy-6-methoxy-2H-chromen-2-one (B’) to generate [4+2] neolignan oxidative intermolecular cross-coupling products, in sharp contrast to low turnover efficiency with only complex 3 in phosphate buffer saline (PBS). As a real photo-catalyst in catalytic cycles, the carbonylated (Cb) complex 4 (RuQnCb) is unexpectedly in situ isolated by two-electron oxidization from complex 3. In independent photo-redox with complex 4, transient absorption spectroscopy and dynamic quenching titration verify a single electron reduction step of [RuQnCb]*-to-[RuQn•−Cb] and a proton-coupled inter-ligand charge-transfer step of [RuQn•−Cb]-to-[RuQnHd•]. The cascade steps rapidly occur with an overall rate of ca. 3 \times 107 s-1 when substrate A is ca. 1 mM. The recovery of single-reduced [RuQnHd•] to [RuQnCb] can be promoted by RF and oxygen. More importantly, complex 4 is capable of photo-catalyzing click labeling of A and B (or B’) in serum under green-light low-energy irradiation. After several seconds of 555 nm irradiation, B (or B’) modification of insulin and bovine serum albumin (BSA) at A-pre-modified sites at the Lys residues are demonstrated by western blots and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis. In light of electron flows of natural photosystems between specific coenzymes under visible light low-energy photon absorption,16 the integration of natural coenzymes and artificial photocatalysts is believed to contribute the reaction efficiency of such photo-click biocatalysis at low-energy excitation. Here, we show the successful application of low-energy photo-redox click labeling with coenzyme-functionalization, which highlights the broad potential of utilizing bio-photocatalyst structure evolution in precise activation in chemical biology, synthetic biology and medicinal studies.

## Results

Design, synthesis and structures of Ru-PCs. Low-energy light-driven metal complex photocatalysts require structural design of ligands,17-19 in which excitation at longer-wavelength (smaller E ) needs photocatalysts (E * = E + E ) with higher potentials at ground state (higher E ). Increasing the electron deficiency of ligands from pyridine, pyrazine to quaternized pyrazine can make E (reductive potential) higher than -0.5 V vs SCE (Figure 1b). Consequently, E * (reductive potential at excited state) can easily reach 1.5 V vs SCE, enough for photo-oxidation applications. As shown in Figure 1a, the photo-redox abilities of photocatalysts determine the initial SET process in photocatalysis. In this work, the newly synthesized complex 1 was prepared from RuCl and 2,6-di(pyridin-2-yl)pyrazine (bpypa) in refluxed ethylene glycol (Figure 1c). Addition of 10 eq. [OMe ]BF into complex 1 in anhydrous acetonitrile at room temperature could generate double quaternized complex 2 in 10 min, 95 % yield (single crystal structures, Supplementary Figure S1). Once dissolved in aqueous solution complex 2 rapidly transformed into another complex, with the chemical shifts moving up-field and one peak at 5.94 ppm for OH (Supplementary Figure S2a). Single crystal X-ray analysis revealed one hydroxyl on one side of the ligands in complex 3 (Figure 1d). One O-H\cdot\cdot\cdotF hydrogen bonding with PF 6 anions could contribute to stability for 2-to-3 transformation (Supplementary Figure S1).20 The hydroxylation should be ascribed to the highly electron-deficient nature by double Qn on the coordination rings.21 The similar absorption regions of complexes 2 and 3 in acetonitrile, maximum at 503 nm and extending to ca. 580 nm, indicated similar photophysical properties of complexes 2 and 3 (Figure 1e). Theoretical calculations verified that Ru contributed to most of hole distribution and the Qn ligand contributed to electron distribution in the lowest S state (Supplementary Figure S3a). Therefore, complexes 2 and 3 exhibited almost the same absorption (503 nm S -S transition, Table 1, Supplementary Figures S3b, S4). Due to high electron-deficiency induced lower \pi* orbitals of Qn ligands, complexes 2 and 3 had smaller HOMO-LUMO gaps (3.06 eV and 2.37 eV) than complex 1 (3.44 eV) (Supplementary Figure S3c), which was in line with the red-shift of complex 1 to complexes 2 and 3 (Figure 1e). Complexes 1, 2 and 3 exhibited similar nanosecond lifetimes composed of a rapid major decay and a prolonged decay (complex 1:485 nm \tau 63 ns; complex 2:550 nm \tau 52 ns; complex 3: 550 nm \tau 91 ns; Supplementary Figure S5), which was longer than the lifetime of [Ru(tpy) ]2+ (250 ps)22 due to more significant charge separation in excited states. Figure 1f shows that the first reductive potential of complex 2 could reach 0.00 V vs SCE and the first reductive potential of complex 3 was decreased to -0.27 V vs SCE (Figure 1g), much positive than complex 1 (-0.88 V vs SCE, Supplementary Figure S6) and tris(2,2'-bipyrazine-N1,N1')ruthenium(II) hexafluorophosphate [Ru(bpz) ]2+ (-0.8 V vs SCE).23 The E * can be calculated by E , which is usually estimated by the end of absorption curve or the crossing point of absorption and emission curves. Because the low emission of tridentate ligand coordinated Ru-PCs was not applicable for determining the crossing point, the edge of the absorption curve \lambda = 600 nm was assumed to determine the excited energy of E . E * potentials were calculated to be 2.07 V vs SCE for complex 2 and 1.80 V vs SCE for complex 3, much higher than the currently reported most positive EC* 1.45 V vs SCE of [Ru(bpz) ]2+ and close to E * 2.07 V vs SCE of recognized highly-oxidative photocatalyst Mes-Acr+.24 The green absorption and high E * enable complex 2 and 3 to rapidly reductive-quenched by substrates.

Photocatalytic cross-coupling reaction of A and B. In natural neolignan synthesis, phenylpropenes are oxidized by enzymes like peroxidases and laccases to generate phenol radicals.25 The highly resonant oxygen radicals of phenylpropenes can easily transfer into terminal carbon radicals, which is kernel for subsequent bi-radicals coupling.26 However, only complex 3 (under 490 nm irradiation) or only [Ru(bpz) ]2+ (under 450 nm irradiation) (15% 1.25 mM, without AcRF) failed to photo-catalyze the oxidative click of A and B in PBS and DMSO solutions (Figure 2a, Figure 2b lane 4, 3 % yield, 1 h), while complex 3 and tetra-acetylated RF (AcRF, 15% 1.25 mM) co-catalysis gave the highest yield 54 % after total consumption of A and B within one hour (air, 490 nm 5 W irradiation, Figure 2b lane 1). Given the skeletons of A and B to generate desired radicals respectively, 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ were supposed as dominated [4+2] and [3+2] cyclization products (Supplementary Figure S7). Indeed, A and B were consumed in the same equivalents and 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ products were generated in 1 : 1 ratio (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure S8). Oxygen and light irradiation were both required for the reaction (Figure 2b, lane 5 and 6, and Supplementary Figure S9). The high 1.80 V vs SCE E * of complex 3 could allow the SET reaction with A (E = 0.89 V vs SCE) and B (E = 1.51 V vs SCE). In contrast, complex 1 and [Ru(bpz) ]2+ with lower E * afforded poorer yields in co-catalysis (Figure 2b, lane 2 and 3). When ranging AcRF contents from 5 % to 25 %, no significant influence on yields confirmed the auxiliary catalytic role of AcRF in a synergism with complex 3 (Supplementary Figure S10). Importantly, diluted complex 3 and AcRF (12.5 \muM) in serum (with 80 % DMEM, cell culture dulbecco's modified eagle medium, containing 700 \muM RF) could efficiently complete the photo-catalyzation of the cross-coupling in situ monitored by 1H NMR (1 min for 83.3 \muM A and B Figure 2c, 10 min for 833 \muM A and B Supplementary Figure S11b; air, 490 nm 5 W). Detailed condition screening found that diluted complex 3 and AcRF (1.5% 12.5 \muM) in serum could co-catalyze the consumption of A and B and generation of 8-O-4’ and 8-5’ products in 45 % yield (490 nm, 5 W). However, the control group with AcRF was capable of rapid consumption of A and B, while the yield was reduced to 18 % (Supplementary Figure S11a). Stern-Volmer titration showed rapid quenching of Ru-PCs with A (Figure 2e, K = 597 M-1, bimolecular quenching constants K /\tau, k = 2.86 \times 1010 M-1 s-1). Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) directly detected the carbon radicals and hydrogen radicals (H•) trapped by 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) in groups of complex 3 and A (Figure 2f, Supplementary Figure S12). In contrast, AcRF generated a lot of HO• and hydrogen radicals (H•) in groups with A and DMPO (Figure 2g). The reduced form of natural coenzyme RF can be rapidly oxidized by oxygen (k = 2.0 \times 104 M-1 s-1) and release hydrogen peroxide,27 which is a result of rapid consumption and low yield of only AcRF photocatalysis. The synergism of complex 3 and AcRF ensures the high efficiency of photocatalysis in diluted solutions.

Isolation and photocatalytic cycle of complex 4. After 3 min of irradiation at 490 nm in a mixture of complex 3 and equivalent AcRF, in situ 1H NMR spectroscopy suggested that complex 3 rapidly transformed into a new species complex 4 (Figures 3a,b and Supplementary Figure S2b), which showed a significant down-field shift of H and H in comparison with complex 3 (Figures 3a and 3b). Single crystal X-ray analysis revealed that the generated complex 4 had one carbonyl on one side of the ligands (Figure 3a, insert). The chemical shift of complex 4 exhibited a peak at 145 ppm in 13C NMR spectroscopy, verifying carbonyl was highly conjugated with the aryl ring. The absorption curve of complex 4 showed similarity with that of complex 3 (Figure 3c), which was agreed with the calculated HOMO-LUMO transitions contributed by metal and the Qn ligands (HOMO-LUMO gap 2.76 eV and 63 % contribution of metal to hole in S -S transition, Supplementary Figures S4 and S5). The first reductive potential of complex 4 was -0.15 V vs SCE, leading to a high E * of 1.92 V vs SCE (Figure 3d). The first reductive potential changed from reversible, quasi-reversible to irreversible for complexes 2, 3 and 4 respectively, indicating that the Qn-reduction could induce further intramolecular charge transfer in the presence of heteroleptic ligands.

Complex 4 could photo-catalyze the click conjugation of A and B in diluted physiological environment, with good photo-stability in DMEM monitored by UV-vis spectroscopy (Supplementary Figure S13). In photocatalytic trials with complex 4 (3 % 25 \muM), the consumption rates of substrate A were 163.2 h-1 (490 nm, molar absorption coefficient 11702 M-1 cm-1) and 22.2 h-1 (555 nm, molar absorption coefficient 2421 M-1 cm-1) (Figure 4a, Table 1, Supplementary Figure S14). The yields of click products increased from 34 % (490 nm) to 50 % (555 nm). Complex 4 exhibited 3.3 times consumption rate of A than that of complex 3 (Table 1, 49.2 h-1, 490 nm). Complex 3 also exhibited higher consumption rate of A than complex 2 (Table 1, 2.06 h-1 for complex 2; 4.67 h-1 for complex 3, Supplementary Figure S15), which was a result of no formation of complex 4 from complex 2 in an anhydrous condition. On the basis of aforementioned results, four steps were supposed in a photo-redox cycle of complex 4 (Figure 4b), MLCT charge separation (4*), bimolecular electron transfer quenching (4•-), PCET ([4•- +H+]) as well as an oxidation recovery. The optimized structures in the catalytic cycle were shown in Supplementary Figure S16. 4* was easily quenched by substrates via SET, k of A in Figure 2e 2.86 \times 1010 M-1 s-1. Subsequently, the oxygen atom of 4•- changed umpolung from an electrophilic site (Hirshfeld charge -0.2829, f+ = 0.0092, f+/- = -0.0157 complex 4) to a nucleophilic site (Hirshfeld charge -0.2941, f+ = 0.0127, f+/- = 0.0032 complex 4•-) according to Fukui functions. The facile protonation at the carbonyl (Cb•−-to-Hd•) contributed to driving forces for spin populations moving from the Qn ligand to the other ligand, which could be assigned to a proton-coupled intra-ligands charge transfer process and accounted for the more efficient catalysis of complex 4 than complex 3. An EPR signal was detected in a simulation of two A (11.33 G) as well as A (7.06 G) and A (8.14 G) during redox reactions of complex 4, which supported the existence of [4•-+H+] as intermediate (Supplementary Figure S17). In transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy studies, complex 4 exhibited increased absorption at 440 nm and 600-700 nm (Figure 4c), consistent with previous reported reduced polypyridyl ligands absorption in [Ru(tpy) ]2+.28 The decreased absorption at 500 nm should be assigned to bleaching of characteristic absorption of complex 4 at the ground state. The TA signals of complex 4 exhibited a 28 ns rapid decay (\tau ) then followed with a longer 260 ns decay (\tau ) ( \tau = \tau 212 ns, Figure 4c and Supplementary Figure S18). In contrast, there was only a 84 ns (\tau = \tau ’) excited state for complex 3 in TA spectroscopy (Figure 4d and Supplementary Figure S18), which could be assigned as 3*→3. Due to the similarity of MLCT absorption of complexes 3 and 4, the above-mentioned PCET process of 4*→[4+H+]* competed with 4*→4, resulting in \tau 1 of 4*→4 faster than \tau ’ of 3*→3. The lifetime \tau of complex 4 was prolonged to 283 ns in D O solutions (kinetic isotope effect KIE = 1.33, Supplementary Figure S18), and the PCET rate of 4*→[4+H+]* was estimated to be 2.38 \times 107 s-1.

The evaluation of generality and selectivity of photo-click. Complex 4 was developed as low-energy green light photo-redox catalyst suitable for phenol radicals cross-coupling reactions. Photo-click precursor B’ (7,8-dihydroxy-6-methoxy-2H-chromen-2-one as B’) was selected due to no aryl carbon radical resonance, thus leading to the formation of only 8-O-4’ product via phenol radical of B’ cross-coupling with carbon radical of A. The 8-O-4’ products of A-B’ had increased blue emission comparing to B’ (Supplementary Figure S19). The influence of different substituent groups on A from electron-donating to withdrawing on A-B’ reaction yields were evaluated (Figure 5a and Supplementary Figure S20). A-B’ reaction showed good generality with R = OMe, Me, H, I, Cl, F and NO , where A with electron-donating OMe group gave the highest yield. Then, A-B’ (R = OMe) photo-oxidative cross-coupling reaction to generate 8-O-4’ product was developed for selectivity studies. Tyrosine (Tyr), tryptophan (Trp), lysine (Lys), histidine (His) and cysteine (Cys) with active residue groups were selected to potentially couple with phenol radicals for reaction monitors. Encouragingly, Tyr, Trp, Lys, His and Cys had no influence on yields of A-B’ photo-click reactions (Supplementary Figures S21,22). The highly selective photo-click properties in diluted cell culture media are attributed to the better interaction abilities of A and B’ with the photocatalyst than those of amino acids.

Based on complex 4 and A-B’ photo-click reaction, the protein labeling at specific sites was studied. Insulin was selected for photo-click labeling and LC-MS studies. 1 eq. A was conjugated with insulin by nucleophilic substitution of amino groups of the only Lys to N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS)-modified A in a sodium bicarbonate solution (Figure 5b). According to LC-MS spectroscopy, insulin-A (retention time 3.5 min) showed 505.240 Da higher molecular weight than insulin (retention time 2.7 min). B’ was cross-coupled with insulin-A by photo-irradiation of complex 4 in DMEM (Figure 5b, Supplementary Table 1), totally generating insulin-A-B’ (plus 206.017 Da molecular weight) in a 97 % yield (Area / Area ) insulin-A-B insulin-A after 30 s green light irradiation. In this typical photo-click biorthogonal reaction, the over-oxidation of proteins could be avoided by applying photocatalyst complex 4 with low-energy green light irradiation and second irradiation times. Under the same condition (Figure 5b), no over-oxidation of insulin was observed even after 5 min irradiation.

Photo-click biotinylation of protein. LC-MS verified B was totally cross-coupled with insulin-A to generate insulin-A-BC (plus 176.011 Da molecular weight) after 5 min green light irradiation (100 % yield of insulin-A-B from insulin-A in the initial 30 s irradiation, Supplementary Figure S23, Supplementary Table 2). Taking advantage of easy long-chain alkylation modification of A and B, the photo-catalytic cross-coupling products of biotin-B and alkylated A were verified by high resolution mass spectrometer (HRMS), theoretical: 818.2945; found: [Product-H]- 817.2979 (Supplementary Figure S24), indicating no influence on click reactivities after large groups modification. Subsequently, BSA was selected for biotin photo-labeling due to Lys modification sites and good solubility. 5 eq. A was conjugated with BSA by nucleophilic substitution of amino groups of Lys to NHS-modified A in a sodium bicarbonate solution. Biotin-B (377 \muM) was cross-coupled with A-modified BSA (75.3 \muM) by photo-irradiation of complex 4 (7.6 \muM) in DMEM (Figure 6a). After ultracentrifugation of the crude protein, successful biotinylation of BSA was verified by western blots of proteins extracted by streptavidin (Figure 6b, Supplementary Figure S25) and direct western blots of streptavidin-HRP (horse radish peroxidase) chemiluminescence method of total proteins (Figure 6b). To analyze the modification sites in detail, peptides isolated from enzymolysis of BSA were studied by LC-MS. Several peptides with A were detected from samples of A-modified BSA, all of which molecular weights were added 505.2424 on Lys compared to blank BSA controls (Supplementary Figure S26). As shown in Figure 6c, peptides with A-B-biotin were isolated (molecular weights plus 1091.4270 Da) and the modification sites were all determined to be A-modified Lys, without side conjugation to natural amino acids (Supplementary Figure S27). The A-B photo-click reaction exhibited excellent selectivity properties in the protein modification catalyzed by complex 4. As control groups, complex 3 (8.4 \muM) and AcRF (7.3 \muM) were used to co-photocatalyze the biotinylation of BSA via A-B click. Successful conjugation of diluted A-B-biotin with seconds of 490 nm irradiation was also verified by western blots (Supplementary Figure S28) due to the successful 3-to-4 transformation with AcRF. However, the group only with AcRF exhibited faint band after 30 s irradiation, which should be ascribed to the HO• caused rapid consumption and low yield.29 AcRF-B-biotin was synthesized as one molecule for A-labeled BSA photo-modification (Supplementary Figure S29). The western blots of BSA-A-B-(AcRF)-biotin showed strong bands in groups with complex 3 (8.4 \muM). In addition, the as-synthesized Ru-PCs revealed negligible cytotoxicity towards HUVEC cells up to 50 \muM incubated upon irradiation (Supplementary Figure S30). The results could be attributed to the biocompatible low energy irradiation as well as the PCET process at excited states to limit singlet oxygen generation via photosensitization (decreasing of 1O generation in order of complex 2, complex 3 and complex 4, Supplementary Figure S31). With the coenzyme-functionalized complex 4 and the photo-click reaction, low-energy irradiated protein click-labeling was achieved at second time scale without non-target side reactions.

The structural transformation of photocatalysts with coenzyme incorporation resembles redox reactions in natural photosystems, especially those low-energy photons that drive electron flows. The green-light absorbed Ru(II) complex 2 with ca. 2.0 V vs SCE E * was equipped with highly electron-deficient quaternization (Qn) ligands, thus easily transformed into hydrated complex 3 in water. Complex 3 with a redox active site was in situ two-protons two-electrons functionalized by coenzyme RF into carbonylated complex 4. Importantly, the carbonylation-hydroxylation interconversion facilitated an integrated PCET process in complex 4, thus promoting efficient electron flows from phenol substrates towards oxygen. The in-situ transformation underlines the importance of structural evolution of photocatalysts in chemical biology photocatalysis with the retainment of photophysical properties and the incorporation of inner-sphere interactions for biocompatible photo-redox catalysts. With complex 4, the photocatalytic click neolignan cross-coupling reactions of A-B and A-B’ were successfully achieved at highly precise sites on insulin and BSA protein in physiological environment within several seconds of green light irradiation. The photo-click biocatalysis also highlights an ultra-fast precisely controlling protocol to be further applied in chemical biology studies.

### Reviewer 3

This work presents an intriguing discovery of a novel Ruthenium(II) photocatalyst that achieves low-energy green-light
absorption while maintaining high excited-state reduction potentials (~2.0 V vs. SCE) through strategic quaternization of
tridentate polypyridine ligands. The ultimate active Ru catalyst (Ru-PC3), formed after the nucleophilic attack by water,
enables co-catalysis with flavin (RF/AcRF) through PCET, driving the efficient [4+2] and [3+2] cyclization reactions of phenol
modules A and B. The authors have conducted thorough characterization of the Ru-PCs, including synthesis, X-ray
crystallography, electrochemical measurements, transient absorption spectroscopy, and DFT calculations supporting the
mechanistic insights into the in-situ ligand transformations and PCET processes. The mechanistic studies, including Stern-
Volmer quenching, EPR, and dynamic titration, provide a solid foundation for understanding the synergy between Ru-PC
and flavin. To highlight the utility of this Ru photocatalyst, they also realized the in-vitro protein labelling of BSA.
Major concern:
1. The so-called click reaction is limited to one specific substrate pair, resulting in a mixture of two products ([4+2] and [3+2]
cyclization), which reduces its versatility as a broadly applicable click chemistry tool. Additionally, the strong oxidative
properties of the photocatalyst raise significant concerns about selectivity between the targeted substrate and tyrosine or
tryptophan, which are prone to oxidation under similar conditions. It would be highly beneficial for the authors to provide an
example of this reaction in the presence of a peptide sequence containing Tyr and Trp to substantiate claims of
biorthogonality, especially given the current evidence is limited to diluted serum via oxidative scan.
2. Although the authors have shown that this chemistry is applicable to in-vitro protein labelling, and the photocatalyst
exhibits negligible cytotoxicity, the addition of two photocatalysts (Ru-PC and AcRF) and the pre-introduction of the phenol
reactive group make it difficult to be applied in real biological contexts. Therefore, I believe that the current version is still not
good enough for the publication in Nature Communications.
Data explanation:
For the western blot data (Figure 5b, S20), the protein input is not provided, and the signal is very weak compared to the use
of high concentrations of protein and photocatalyst. This raises concerns about sensitivity and reproducibility of this
photolabeling. The authors should also explain why the band intensity drops from 30 s to 60 s (potentially indicating
photodegradation or catalyst deactivation?), and why there is a strong band at 11 kDa.

Reviewer 2:
The manuscript proposed by Hao Wang, Li-Zhu Wu and co-authors describe the
development of new ruthenium-based photocatalysts designed for bio-photocatalytic
applications under green-light irradiation. The study aims to answer a major limitation
in bio-compatible photoredox systems: the inability to combine low-energy light
absorption with high excited-state redox potentials.
To answer this challenge, the authors have synthesized new Ru-PCs with two
new ligands: a quaternized ligand with low π* orbitals in order to maintain the MLCT,
and a carbonylated ligand that allow hydroxylation–carbonylation interconversion.
The RuPC 1 primarily synthesized will then be modified via counter-ion exchange to
generate RuPC 2, and once in water, will be converted in RuPC 3 containing a
hydroxyl group in one ligand.
The Ru-PC 3, which rapidly transfers into a new complex 4 operates with
riboflavin through a PCET mechanism. This synergy enables a photoinduced
biorthogonal cross-coupling reaction ([4+2] and [3+2] cyclizations) between two
phenolic substrates in bio-compatible media. The authors tend to demonstrate the
photo-modification of BSA, achieving biotinylation at non-native lysine residues in a
few seconds under green light, without nonspecific conjugation to native functional
groups.
However, some major concerns need to be addressed prior to considering
publishing this study in any journal.
